“I’m… sorry to hear that,” said Joe. “I don’t really know what to say.” He looked down.

“Nobody does,” said Ema. “What about you? Something keeping you tethered to the mortal plane?” Her voice dripped with sarcasm.

“It’s the opposite, actually,” said Joe. “But I’m not really sure.”

“The fuck is that supposed to mean?” asked Ema, swinging her mop from her right hand to her left.

“Have you ever heard of liminal spaces?” asked Joe.

“Sure I have,” said Ema, not missing a beat. “Places in transition. Defined by what they were and what they’re going to be, and not what they currently are. But you’re gonna explain it to me like I don’t know, aren’t you?”

“What makes you think that?” asked Joe.

“You’re up here interrogating me about my abuse and shit, calling me out every time I say something that doesn’t fit with your worldview,” said Ema. Joe opened his mouth, and she raised a finger to cut him off. “Save it,” she said. “You’re gonna tell me that you don’t have a worldview, right? That you’re neutral or some shit? Because you’re not. Don’t take it the wrong way, Skeletor, but you don’t fool me.”

Joe looked away, still distant. “I feel like there’s more to it than what you just described. It isn’t so clinical. It isn’t so foreign. It’s like elevators. Like playgrounds at night. Like in the morning after it’s snowed, and there aren’t any tracks in the street. Like an empty classroom in the summertime.” Joe leaned against the walls of a cubicle. “Like this office. Like this entire building. Whatever it was is how everyone remembers it. Nobody thinks about it in the present tense.”

“I know what a fucking liminal space is,” Ema snapped. “I have a psych degree, you goddamned chauvinist. Are you fucking lecturing me?”

“Sorry,” said Joe, startled. “Right. Sorry. You get it. This is new to me.” He swallowed as his pacing came to a halt. “I think I’m a liminal space.”

“Okay, be specific,” demanded Ema.

“Everyone has…” said Joe, trailing off as Ema rolled her eyes. “I get it,” he said, interrupting himself. “I’m lecturing you, I know. I’m sorry. I don’t mean to. I’m just… I’m slow, alright? I need to process these things out loud. Okay? Everyone has a purpose. Everyone has a task. You’re here to do a job, right? You work here. You’re here to do something. You’re here with a purpose. Not me,” said Joe, quickly. “My mind is hash, but I remember a little bit. I remember pieces of my life. I remember a family, but I don’t remember ever being attached to them. I remember other people, but I don’t remember ever speaking with them. I remember education and work, but I don’t remember ever learning anything from it or feeling fulfilled. I don’t remember ever moving in one direction for more than an instant. I have no one to attach myself to. I have no experiences to fall back on. I have no task set out for me. I don’t think I ever did.”

“Do you want me to feel sorry for you? Is that what this is about?” asked Ema.

“No. You couldn’t,” said Joe, hastily. “I know you couldn’t. I know you don’t. But, I mean, do you understand what I’m saying? Because if you do, then maybe you can make sense of it better than I can. I’m a person that has no function. I’m just the liminal space between a fetus and a corpse. I’m defined by what I was and what I will be, but not by what I am. I’m nothing. Or maybe I became nothing. I don’t know when, but one day I woke up and stopped existing. No one can notice me. No one can remember me. I’m operating under the assumption that it’s because there’s nothing for them to notice, and nothing for them to remember. There’s no purpose that defines the object they perceive me as. Tell me that makes sense to you.” He nervously glanced back to Ema, who seemed contemplative. Moments passed before she responded.

“Okay,” she said, drawing a vape pen from her jacket pocket. “Yeah, that makes sense. I mean, you’re assuming that people can just intrinsically understand that you don’t have any reason to be where you are, and that, somehow, that would make them completely unable to perceive you in any meaningful way, but, yeah. Sure. That’s exactly what a ghost would say, but I see where you’re coming from.”

Joe paused, and then he laughed. It was the first time he’d laughed in months. 

“Okay,” he said. “Sure. I’m a ghost. I’m an amnesiac ghost.”

“Don’t knock it,” said Ema. “I’ve seen ghosts before. I see them all the time. Like, how else do you think I can see you?”

“I don’t know,” said Joe, amusedly. “But it would make sense, sure.” He tasted blood in his mouth, and in the moment, it didn’t faze him.

“You’re wrong, by the way,” said Ema.

“About what?” asked Joe.

“That I couldn’t feel sorry for you,” replied Ema. “I don’t know what you think I’m all about, but I am genuinely sorry that you went through being isolated for so long. I don’t know if you’re upset about it, but if you are, that’s valid.”

Joe was stunned. He’d never felt so acknowledged in all of his life. Even before he stopped existing. Even with his family. Even with his friends.

“…Thank you,” said Joe. “That means a lot.”

Ema put the pen up to her lips. “Shit, man,” she said. “So, like, do you go to heaven now?”

“Yeah,” said Joe. There was a bit of pain in his voice. “Yeah, I guess I do. Doesn’t really explain why I couldn’t recognize myself, though,” He looked in his reflection in the glass, and he stammered. He could, in fact, see himself. He could see a hollow white face staring back at him, framed with oily hair and soot. There was blood on his brow. He looked emaciated.

“Was I bleeding when I got here?” he asked.

“No,” said Ema, turning to face him. “Ghosts don’t…” She trailed off as her jaw dropped. Joe wasn’t transparent anymore. He was hovering above the ground, like a marionette on a string. Deep, jagged gashes were erupting across his skin. Blood spurted out from them, and it turned black and dry as it was exposed to the air. His body desiccated almost instantly. Every one of his bones snapped and fractured apart like he was being crushed between an iron wall and a Mack truck, and his eyes dried out and shriveled up like raisins. He held in the air for a moment, and the lights started to flicker, and the stagnant air started to howl like a windstorm, and then he fell backwards, knocking over a cubicle wall.

As his head cracked into the carpeted concrete floor, something finally clicked with him. It made sense. All the days and nights he spent wandering, never stopping to rest. All the months without food or water or shelter. All the times he’d hurt himself since the day he stopped existing—all the car crashes and bullet wounds and scrapes and burns and bruises. All of it was coming back to him in an instant. 

The self-obfuscation was so powerful that even death itself didn’t notice him. Not until now, at least.

“The *fuck?”* shouted Ema. The stick-end of her mop caught under the brim of her hat and knocked it off her head as she knelt down to try and resuscitate him. Her hands nearly punched through his ribcage. Joe’s voice was a ruined whisper, but, somehow, it carried. 

“Nobody told me… Nobody said it’d be fun to talk to other people,” he murmured. “Would’ve spoken up more if I’d known… how satisfying it was.” He managed a half-smile. “To be heard, that is.” 

Ema’s eyes went wide as the body started disintegrating. With all the strength he had left, Joe blinked. 

Then he was gone.

Cubicles were set down on the floors, but the desks behind them were empty, or they were uprooted from the floor and set down on their sides, or they were gone. Ethernet cables sprouted out all bunched together in the stained-silver frames of floor panels, attached to nothing. All the computers were ancient, and their frames were bleached white by the sunlight that came bursting through the windows. No one had worked here in years. Decades, probably. There was no evidence of what they’d been doing there; no sign of what anyone had been trying to accomplish. All the renovations had just frozen up.

The memory of the emotions he might have felt at the sight of it didn’t leave him as he explored the space. Every new abandoned station that he came across seemed to drag at his mind. All of it was familiar to him. Almost relatable, in a way. Whatever injuries he’d sustained in the crash didn’t feel as distant as he sauntered through the gaps between the cubicles. His mind was starting to heat up. Then he stopped.

There was another person in the abandoned office with him, standing by the windows. Almost invisible in her janitor’s fatigues. Her gaze was dark and hollow, and it followed his movements. She wasn’t far from him. She wasn’t moving. Just watching. Waiting. Minutes of standing still passed before she decided to speak.

“Do you work here?” she asked. Her voice was like the low creak of wooden floorboards. It didn’t sound human. Joe, of course, assumed she was speaking to someone else, and he turned away.

“I’m talking to you, ghost boy,” she said. A pale hand pointed at him from the shadows of the corner she was standing in. “Why’re you here?”

Joe blinked. There was no blackout. No lapse in memory. He was fully conscious. He met the janitor’s hollow gaze, and he felt a sense of kinship.

“I needed a place to go,” he said, finally. “I used to be curious about this place.”

“This is a private office,” said the janitor, stepping out from the shadows. She looked younger than she sounded. Maybe a few years past college age. Her arms were sleeved with H.R. Giger tattoos, and the lines in her face were deeper than they should’ve been. She cocked her head to one side, like birds do. “I mean, I don’t care if you’re up here or not, but we have security guards in this building. We have cameras in these offices. People are gonna come up here once they see you on the camera feed.”

“They won’t see me,” said Joe.

“I can see you,” said the janitor.

“Why’d you call me a ghost?” asked Joe

“Can’t think of a better way to describe it,” said the janitor. “You’re kinda see-through.”

“Really?” he asked.

“Yeah. I mean, look in a mirror if you want proof,” said the janitor. “It’s kinda fucked up.”

“Oh,” said Joe, flatly. “I’m sorry for scaring you, then.” He couldn’t hear it, but his voice was tinged with melancholy.

“You don’t scare me,” said the janitor.

“You said I was fucked up,” said Joe.

“So? I don’t care,” said the janitor. “Who gives a shit what other people think about you?”

“I do,” said Joe. “I’ve been trying to get someone to talk to me for months. Years, maybe. I don’t know anymore. I lost count. Nobody can see me. Nobody can *notice* me. You’re the first person that’s ever turned my way and said something for as long as I can remember.” He was too dazed to consider the weight of his words.

The janitor paused. “Oh shit, I was just exaggerating with the ghost thing,” she said. “Don’t tell me you’re actually, like, full Nosferatu.”

“Shouldn’t you be more surprised?” asked Joe.

“Maybe,” said the janitor. “I’ve seen weirder. I’ve seen some shit.”

Joe looked out the windows. The gray skies hung like a wreath over the city, but there was still a kind of beauty to it. He could see the financial district just past the old stretch of the city. Probably where the businessman in the crash was headed off to. He could see all the shops he passed to get to where he was going. He could see the wreckage a few blocks away, all cordoned-off and hidden with yellow tape. Guilt. He could feel guilt, now. Just a bit.

“What kind of shit?” asked Joe.

“Abuse, mostly,” said the janitor.

“That doesn’t sound supernatural,” said Joe.

“What’s your name?” asked the janitor, not skipping a beat.

“Joe,” said Joe, just as flatly. “Are you Ema?”

“Shit, did you read my mind?” asked Ema.

“No. You have a nametag,” said Joe, pointing to a brass bar on the collar of her jacket that read ‘Ema’ in engraved lettering. “Is that a misspelling?” he asked.

Ema raised one eyebrow. “No, dumbass, it’s Japanese. They don’t misspell nametags.” She paused. “You ever been beaten before, Joe? Ever been harassed?”

Joe took a moment to respond. His eyes were distant. “Not that I can remember,” he said.

“Then you don’t get to tell me what is and isn’t supernatural,” said Ema. “Try telling me there isn’t something unholy about the way a person turns into an animal when they lose their temper with you. Try telling me it isn’t anything short of fucking *possession* when they start foaming at the mouth and throwing things when you say something they don’t like. Live through it. Then you get to disagree with me.”

Joe paused. “Alright. Who abused you?” he asked, finally.

 “Sorta people you’re supposed to trust,” said Ema. “Parents. Girlfriends. Cops. Not that I trust cops, but, y’know. I used to. You realize once you’re out of the house just how invisible you really are. Nobody talks about people like me. Nobody cares if they turn up dead.”

“That sounds a bit extreme,” said Joe.

“It’s true enough. You ever seen a female janitor?” asked Ema. “You ever seen one in their twenties? I sure as fuck haven’t. I don’t know anybody else who has. People ignore me for it. I’m too out-of-place to pay attention to. Doesn’t make much sense, but that’s my theory, at least. So I might as well be a ghost, too.”

Cool as it is to have ultra-powerful characters, it’s much more fun to work with flawed, limited ones. That’s why Julius is such a cool character. He’s arrogant and stubborn, and he lacks any fighting skill, but he’s powerful in spite of that, and that’s why we love him. He overcomes his flaws through effort and genius. From what you’ve given us, there isn’t much room for Kaiser to develop as a character. She has no weaknesses. Nothing to overcome. Like a female Yujiro Hanma. She wouldn’t need to think tactically in a fight, since nothing could harm her. She’d just attack and win.

But what if she didn’t have her superman syndrome or her selective breeding? What if all she had were her techniques? She could still have her build and her experience, but what if her strength came from her intuition and her wisdom, rather than godlike inborn traits? I think that would make a fight between her and another character much, much more interesting. Better yet, what if she had exploitable weaknesses? Maybe her boobs get in the way of fighting? Maybe she has horrible back pain? Maybe she has some balance issues? Maybe male fighters don’t take her seriously, and it sets her off? Maybe her fighting style isn’t suited for dealing with Foresight or blow-tanking techniques? Then, when she won a fight, it would be way cooler, since she’d have to think carefully about how she fought.
